analysis.one_liner: Blocks any federal limits on carbon dioxide pollution until China, India, and Russia cut theirs.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with no cosponsors, was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee in January 2013 and never advanced further before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have prohibited the EPA and every other federal agency from regulating carbon dioxide emissions until the Commerce Department certified in writing that China, India, and Russia had begun requiring carbon cuts substantially similar to those proposed for the United States. In practice, it would have stripped the government of its main legal tool for limiting greenhouse gas pollution, since the United States cannot force China, India, or Russia to act. Senator David Vitter introduced it alone; it was sent to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee and never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the main beneficiaries would be coal, oil, and natural gas producers and the power plants and industrial facilities that burn fossil fuels, because it would have blocked the EPA rules that require them to limit carbon emissions. Owners of those assets would avoid compliance costs, and no cleaner substitute (such as expanded renewables or efficiency programs) was offered in the bill to fill the gap. Ordinary people would not have gained a new protection from it; the bill's only operative effect was to remove an existing regulatory obligation from emitters.

how_it_helps.text: The bill prohibited the EPA and the head of any other federal agency from regulating carbon dioxide emissions, which would have blocked pending and future greenhouse gas rules covering power plants and other large emitters.

The prohibition would have stayed in force until the Secretary of Commerce certified that China, India, and Russia had each initiated carbon reduction measures 'substantially similar' to those proposed for the United States — a certification the United States cannot compel three foreign governments to trigger, so the block could have lasted indefinitely.

analysis.who_pays: If it had passed, the costs would have fallen on people exposed to higher carbon pollution: communities near coal plants, and ultimately everyone, since unchecked greenhouse gas emissions drive climate-related damage — worse heat, storms, crop stress, and health harms. Because the bill offered no alternative program (no clean energy support, no efficiency push, no adaptation funding), the burden of unregulated emissions would simply have shifted onto the public and future taxpayers rather than onto emitters.

drawbacks.text: The strongest good-faith argument for the bill is fairness: the United States would bear the cost of cutting emissions while China — the world's largest carbon emitter — India, and Russia faced no comparable requirement, so some US jobs in energy-intensive industries could shift overseas without meaningfully lowering global emissions.

The bill had no fallback: if the foreign certification never came (which its own terms made likely, since it required India, Russia, and China to act in a way no US law can compel), all federal carbon regulation would simply lapse, leaving US emissions unregulated without any domestic plan to address them.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's premise — that other major emitters should carry some of the burden — is a real argument in climate policy. But the bill as written was not a bargaining tool or a substitute plan: it would have repealed the EPA's authority to limit carbon pollution with no replacement program, and its trigger (certification that three foreign governments act) was outside US control, so it functioned as an indefinite block on domestic rules. The costs of unregulated emissions would have outweighed any competitive relief for fossil-fuel-intensive industries, and there is no evidence in the record of a companion program to offset the lost regulation.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced by a single senator, sent to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, and stayed there — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor vote — until the Congress ended in January 2015.

narrative.text: Senator David Vitter of Louisiana introduced the bill on January 23, 2013; it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works.
The committee took no further action, and the full action history shows no vote was ever held in either chamber.
The bill died when the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never advanced, EPA carbon rules remained in place and the fossil-fuel industries it would have shielded gained nothing. Ordinary people and communities exposed to pollution were better off than they would have been under the bill, which offered no replacement for the rules it would have voided.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Coal and oil industries gained nothing

for.name: Sen. David Vitter
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill alone and referred it to the Environment and Public Works Committee.

against.name: Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works
against.role: Committee of referral (chaired by Sen. Barbara Boxer, D-CA, in the 113th Congress)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill, leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

against.name: 0 Senate cosponsors
against.what_they_did: No senator from either party signed on as a cosponsor, so the bill had no visible coalition to push it out of committee.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Republican sponsor, zero cosponsors of either party, and no recorded votes, so its support was confined to one member of the Senate's Republican minority.

industries.industry: Coal producers and coal-fired power plants
industries.note: The bill would have blocked the EPA rules that cap their carbon emissions, letting them avoid compliance costs. The cost of those avoided emissions would fall on the public through pollution and climate damage, so their gain runs against ordinary people's interest.

By prohibiting any federal agency from regulating carbon dioxide, the bill would have exempted oil and gas operations from greenhouse gas limits. Their interest in this bill ran opposite to the public's interest in lower emissions.

A permanent block on carbon regulation would have removed the policy driver for demand for wind, solar, efficiency, and pollution-control equipment. Their loss would have come alongside the public's exposure to unregulated emissions.
